title: Boundaries in friendships
answer: Friends need boundaries too. A good friend respects when you say you do not want to share something, lend money, skip class, drink, or be touched in a certain way. It is okay to tell a friend 'I'm not comfortable with that' or 'please don't share my secrets'. A friend who mocks, threatens or keeps pushing after you say no is not respecting you. Healthy friendships feel safe, equal and kind. A teacher or counsellor can help if a friendship feels harmful.

title: Partner checking your phone and passwords
answer: You have a right to privacy, even in a relationship. A partner demanding your passwords, reading your messages, checking your call history, or telling you who you can chat with is crossing a digital boundary. It can be a sign of control, not love. Trust in a healthy relationship is built by honesty and respect, not by spying. You can say 'my phone is private'. If a partner threatens or punishes you for this, it is a warning sign; call 3512 for advice.

answer: In Rwandan culture, young people are taught to respect elders, and that is a good value. But respect never means letting someone touch you sexually, hurt you or force you into something. Protecting your body is not disrespect. You can be polite and still say no, move away and tell another trusted adult. Good elders want children to be safe. If an older person abuses that respect, help is available from 116, 3512 or a school or community focal person.

title: Privacy when bathing and changing

If someone keeps spying, filming, or insisting on being present when it is not needed, it is a warning sign and should be told to a trusted adult or reported to 116.

title: What is sexual abuse
answer: Sexual abuse is any sexual act or contact that a person does not agree to, cannot agree to, or is forced, tricked or pressured into. It includes unwanted touching, rape, forcing someone to touch another person, showing sexual images, sexual comments or messages, and taking sexual photos. Any sexual activity with a child is abuse. Abuse can be done by strangers, but most often by someone the person knows. It is never the victim's fault. Help: 116, 3512 or Isange on 3029.

title: What is child sexual abuse
answer: Child sexual abuse is when an adult, or an older or more powerful young person, involves a child (anyone under 18) in sexual activity. A child cannot consent to sex, so it is always abuse, even if the child seemed to agree or did not resist. It includes touching, rape, showing sexual images, making sexual photos or videos, and sexual talk. It is a serious crime in Rwanda. The child is never to blame. Report it to 116, 3512, Isange (3029) or police on 112.

answer: Many abused children stay silent. They may be threatened, told it is a secret, or afraid no one will believe them. This is why adults should ask gently, listen, and believe children. Silence does not mean nothing happened. Help is available on 116 and 3512.

title: What is incest
answer: Incest is sexual activity between close family members, such as a parent and child, siblings, or a grandparent and grandchild. When it involves a child, it is sexual abuse. Anyone who knows about incest can seek help from 116, 3512, Isange (3029) or the police on 112.

title: Sexual abuse by teachers
answer: Teachers have a duty to protect students. Any sexual touching, sexual messages, requests for sex, or relationships between a teacher and a student are abuse of power and are not allowed. This includes asking a student to stay alone after class for sexual reasons or offering marks, money or favours. Students are never to blame. It can be reported to the head teacher, a school focal person, parents, 116, 3512 or RIB. A student can bring a friend when reporting.

answer: Neighbours are often trusted and children may visit their homes, run errands or watch TV there. title: Emotional effects of sexual abuse
answer: Sexual abuse can affect feelings for a long time. Survivors may feel fear, shame, guilt, anger, sadness, numbness or confusion. They may have nightmares, trouble sleeping or concentrating, avoid certain places, or lose trust in people. Some feel nothing at first. All these reactions are normal responses to something harmful. They are not a sign of weakness. Counselling and support really help. Isange One Stop Centres (3029) offer psychosocial support, and 3512 or 116 can link survivors to help.

title: Healing after abuse is possible
answer: Many survivors of sexual abuse go on to live happy, healthy lives. Healing takes time and looks different for each person. It helps to talk to someone safe, get counselling, keep up routines, rest, and spend time with supportive people. Some days will be harder than others, and that is normal. What happened does not define a person's worth or future. Isange One Stop Centres (3029), health centres and counsellors offer support, and 116 or 3512 can guide you.

title: What is rape
answer: Rape is when someone forces or tricks another person into sexual intercourse, or any sexual penetration, without their consent. It includes using force, threats, drugs, alcohol, or taking advantage of someone who is asleep, very drunk, or too young to consent. Rape can happen to girls, boys, women and men, and by strangers, partners or family members. It is a serious crime in Rwanda. It is never the victim's fault. Help: Isange 3029, GBV line 3512, or 112.

title: What is grooming
answer: Grooming is when someone builds trust and an emotional connection with a child or young person, and sometimes their family, so they can later abuse or exploit them. A groomer may give gifts, attention, compliments, money or special favours, then slowly introduce secrecy, sexual talk or touching. It can happen in person or online and can take weeks or months. Grooming is a form of abuse. If something feels wrong, tell a trusted adult or call 116.
